recent_posts.title: How to install Arch Linux manually with GNOME from scratch
recent_posts.summary: A complete step-by-step walkthrough for manually installing Arch Linux on real hardware (AMD ThinkPad). Covers downloading and verifying the ISO, flashing to USB, disabling Secure Boot, partitioning with cfdisk (EFI, root, swap, home), formatting, mounting, installing base packages with pacstrap, generating fstab, configuring timezone/locale/hostname, setting up users and sudo, installing and configuring GRUB bootloader, and finishing with GNOME desktop environment. Also includes optional SSH remote installation, mirror optimization with reflector, Bluetooth setup, and post-install system update.

recent_posts.title: Comparing Bash, ZSH, and Fish shells for scripting and interactive use
recent_posts.summary: Bash, ZSH, and Fish are three popular terminal shells with distinct strengths. Bash is widely installed and ideal for writing portable shell scripts due to its universal availability. ZSH offers similar syntax to Bash but excels in interactive use with extensive plugin support for features like auto-suggestions, syntax highlighting, and customizable prompts. Fish provides the most user-friendly experience out-of-the-box with built-in auto-suggestions and syntax highlighting, though it uses different syntax that's easier to learn but less portable. For public scripts, use Bash; for interactive terminal work, choose ZSH (if you enjoy customization) or Fish (if you want minimal configuration).

recent_posts.title: Getting started with FZF fuzzy finder for terminal productivity
recent_posts.summary: FZF is a powerful fuzzy finder for the terminal that enables quick filtering through files, directories, command history, and any list-based data. It supports fuzzy search patterns, exact matches, prefix/suffix searches, and multi-select mode. Key features include keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+T for files, Ctrl+R for command history, Alt+C for directories), integration with common commands like git, kill, and text editors, and simple installation via Git. The tool significantly improves terminal productivity by making navigation and command execution faster and more intuitive.

recent_posts.title: Switching from macOS to Linux for software development
recent_posts.summary: A Mac developer shares their experience transitioning to Linux for software development by setting up Ubuntu in a virtual machine. The setup includes the i3 tiling window manager, Polybar menu bar, and various terminal tools like Wezterm, Neovim, and Zsh with plugins. While ARM architecture limitations caused some compatibility issues with apps like Spotify, the experience highlighted Linux's superior customization and control compared to macOS. The author plans to continue using Linux for development work and eventually transition to a dedicated x86 machine.

recent_posts.title: Why I Use Only One Monitor
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their transition from multi-monitor setups to a single 27-inch display, citing ergonomic benefits and reduced neck pain. The workflow relies on keyboard shortcuts via Raycast and window management tools to quickly switch between applications and workspaces. This approach eliminates physical screen switching, improves focus by displaying one application at a time, and creates a minimal desk setup. The solution works particularly well on macOS, though the author plans to explore Linux tiling window managers for potentially better results.

Setting up OpenCode AI agent with Neovim and Tmux
recent_posts.summary: OpenCode is an AI coding agent for terminal-based workflows that integrates seamlessly with Neovim and Tmux. It provides contextual code assistance by analyzing entire codebases, supports multiple AI models including Claude and OpenAI, and offers two main agents: plan (for questions and suggestions) and build (for making actual changes). Key features include custom command creation, configurable keybindings, conversation sharing, and undo/redo functionality for AI-generated changes.
